extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the MPEP two-step analysis (statutory category + judicial exceptions/practical application). Intended to direct examiner determinations and advise applicants on claim drafting and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter); and (2) the claim must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas) unless it is a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-step analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exceptions/practical application) to evaluate eligibility. Conduct both steps even if Step 1 appears to fail, since amendment might cure Step 1 and Step 2 analysis still informs examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Process
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is an act, or a series of acts or steps (a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result). See cases such as Gottschalk v. Benson and Bilski v. Kappos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be statutory under §101, a process claim must be directed to a particular practical application and not merely recite an abstract idea; see §100(b) and MPEP §2106.01 for processes involving laws of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices; includes mechanical devices or combinations of devices to perform functions and produce effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting a machine with tangible elements that work together in a defined combination will generally be within the machine category; however, mere recitation of a machine without tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may fail to show a practical application of an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture is an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations (regardless of whether by hand or machinery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to articles produced from materials that embody a tangible practical application fall within this category; tangible structural limitations are evidence of a particular practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions of matter include compositions of two or more substances and composite articles (chemical unions, mixtures, gases, fluids, powders, solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A composition that is a non-naturally occurring practical embodiment is generally statutory, subject to exceptions for natural products or phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory example embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain things are non-statutory and not patent-eligible as claimed per se, e.g., transitory forms of signal transmission (a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), naturally occurring organisms, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examples and case citations (e.g., In re Nuijten, Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Miller) illustrate these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (in light of the specification and a person skilled in the art) covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 when claim scope includes non-statutory embodiments (e.g., a computer readable medium that can be a compact disc or a carrier wave). Consider whether amendment could limit the claim to statutory embodiments; nevertheless, still perform Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions — identification and practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions to §101 include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas (also described using terms like natural phenomena, scientific principles, systems depending on human intelligence alone, disembodied mathematical algorithms, mental processes). Claims wholly directed to these exceptions are not eligible unless limited to a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it is merely directed to an exception or to a particular practical application (which may be eligible). Practical application relates to how the judicial exception is applied in a real-world product or process and whether the claim preempts substantially all uses of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application criterion for product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed product is within one of the product categories and does not recite a judicial exception, it is eligible. If a judicial exception is recited, determine if the exception has been practically applied in the product — tangible embodiments that embody a specific practical application support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible structural limitations (e.g., a cup, magnetic door latch) indicate practical application; claims that recite product-type language but lack tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may be construed to wholly embrace a concept and be ineligible. After finding a practical application, evaluate preemption (does the claim cover substantially all practical applications of the exception?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application criterion for method/process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim, to be statutory under §101, must be limited to a particular practical application; merely claiming an abstract idea or preempting substantially all uses of a law of nature or physical phenomenon is ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool (but not the sole test). Consider whether the claim recites structure or a transformative step and whether additional limitations are insignificant post-solution activity (field-of-use) or meaningless data-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for abstract idea determination — machine/apparatus involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: One factor to consider is whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus. For computer-implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the claimed steps, effectively becoming a special-purpose computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh: (a) particularity/generality of machine elements (is the machine specifically identified?), (b) whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use vs. mere object of operation), and (c) whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation. Mere recitation of 'the Internet' or general-purpose computer without how it aids the method is insufficient. Adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without showing significance to performance is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for abstract idea determination — transformation of an article
rubrics_metrics.description: Another useful factor (from the machine-or-transformation test) is whether the claimed process transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim satisfies machine-or-transformation criteria (tied to a particular machine or transforms an article), it is less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea; but failure to satisfy these inquiries does not automatically render a claim abstract — consider all factors and the claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of multiple factors; field-of-use and extra-solution limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine eligibility by weighing multiple relevant factors (machine implementation, transformation, practical application evidence). Field-of-use limitations do not impose meaningful claim boundaries, and insignificant 'extra-solution' activity (e.g., routine data gathering) does not save a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both factors favoring eligibility (e.g., satisfying machine-or-transformation or practical application evidence) and factors weighing against it. Do not base a conclusion solely on one factor while ignoring others; recognize that new factors may develop with emerging technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for claims to laws of nature or natural correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: When Inquiries indicate the claim does not amount to a patent-eligible practical application (fails Inquiry 3 / integration), the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not being drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making the rejection, identify the natural principle, explain that the claim is effectively directed to the principle itself, and explain why additional features or their combination fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to add significantly more than the principle itself. Provide a clear factual and legal basis (example rejection language and analysis are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating and responding to a subject-matter-rejection — applicant actions that can overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response may include amendments that add steps/features (or amend existing ones) that integrate the natural principle into the process so the claim practically applies the principle, or persuasive arguments that existing steps add something significantly more and are not routine/conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments should add limitations that confine the application beyond mere high-level application (e.g., constructing a specific device that integrates a natural principle rather than merely applying it). Arguments that steps are unconventional or non-routine can be persuasive. Examples: adding a UV sanitizing device structure rather than simply exposing to sunlight; specifying a nonconventional testing technique rather than routine blood testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedential case law and evolving factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance expects examiners to consider Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Diehr, Bilski, Mayo, Myriad, etc.) and recognizes that the factors enumerated are illustrative and may be modified to accommodate developments in case law and emerging technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the machine-or-transformation test as an investigative clue and adapt the weight of factors consistent with evolving precedents; be open to new factors and technology-specific considerations when making eligibility determinations.
